Missing not at random verification

Source: R/verification.R
mnar.Rd

mnar() is the assumption that verification depends on the test results and also on the disease status (Kosinski and Barnhart, 2003a): among subjects with the same profile, diseased and healthy subjects can be verified with different probabilities. Its arguments are the prior on the log odds ratio of verification, the prior on the verification intercepts and the choice of whether the odds ratio varies across profiles.

Usage

mnar(
  odds_ratio_prior = prior_normal(0, 1),
  intercepts_prior = prior_normal(0, 1.5),
  by_profile = FALSE
)

Arguments

odds_ratio_prior

Prior on \(\beta\), the log odds ratio of verification between diseased and healthy subjects with the same profile. It must act on the real line, such as prior_normal() or prior_student(); a prior on a probability, such as prior_beta(), is not accepted. The default prior_normal(0, 1) centres \(\beta\) at 0, which is missing at random, and gives 95% of its prior mass to odds ratios between about 0.14 and 7.1.

intercepts_prior

Prior on the verification intercepts \(\alpha_t\), one for each profile with at least one verified subject. It must act on the real line, as for odds_ratio_prior. It is used only by the log-linear and the random-effects models; the saturated model does not use it. The default prior_normal(0, 1.5) is close to a uniform distribution on the verification probability of healthy subjects, \(\mathrm{expit}(\alpha_t)\). A wider prior, such as prior_normal(0, 2.5), puts about a third of its mass on probabilities below 0.08 or above 0.92; with profiles in which few subjects are verified, it often leads to profiles with subjects but no verified subject, which the model treats as never verified (with a warning from baysesp()).

by_profile

A single logical value, TRUE or FALSE, with default FALSE. If FALSE, one \(\beta\) is shared by all profiles with at least one verified subject, so the odds ratio of verification is the same for every profile. If TRUE, each of these profiles has its own \(\beta_t\), all with prior odds_ratio_prior, so the odds ratio may differ across profiles. Profiles with no verified subject have no \(\beta\).

Value

An object of class mnar.

Details

Let \(V = 1\) indicate that a subject is verified, \(T\) be the response profile, \(D\) the disease status, and \(\lambda_{t,d} = P(V = 1 \mid T = t, D = d)\). The model is $$\mathrm{logit}\,\lambda_{t,d} = \alpha_t + \beta d, \qquad d \in \{0, 1\}.$$ For each profile \(t\) with at least one verified subject, \(\alpha_t\) is the log odds of verification for healthy subjects with profile \(t\), and \(\alpha_t + \beta\) is the log odds of verification for diseased subjects with the same profile. Profiles with no verified subject have \(\lambda_{t,d} = 0\) and no intercept; in the log-linear and random effects models baysesp() warns when such a profile has subjects, because for it verification is then not missing not at random.

\(\beta\) is the log odds ratio of verification between diseased and healthy subjects with the same profile: $$\beta = \log \frac{\lambda_{t,1}\,/\,(1 - \lambda_{t,1})}{\lambda_{t,0}\,/\,(1 - \lambda_{t,0})}.$$ Equivalently, \(\exp(-\beta)\) is the odds ratio of disease between unverified and verified subjects with the same profile. When \(\beta = 0\) verification does not depend on the disease status given the profile, which is the missing at random assumption. A positive \(\beta\) means that diseased subjects are verified more often than healthy subjects with the same profile, so that unverified subjects are less often diseased than verified ones with the same profile; a negative \(\beta\) has the opposite meaning.

With \(\pi = P(D = 1)\) and \(\theta_{d,t} = P(T = t \mid D = d)\) the disease parameters, and \(n_{t,d}\), \(u_t\), \(\pi_1 = \pi\), \(\pi_0 = 1 - \pi\) as in the counts of the observed data, the log-likelihood is $$\ell = \sum_t \Big[\sum_d n_{t,d} \log(\pi_d\,\theta_{d,t}\,\lambda_{t,d}) + u_t \log \sum_d \pi_d\,\theta_{d,t}\,(1 - \lambda_{t,d})\Big].$$

With a saturated disease model, which places no restriction on \(\theta_d\), the data identify the proportion of diseased among verified subjects of each profile, but not \(\beta\). The proportion of diseased among unverified subjects with a verified profile \(t\) is \(\mathrm{expit}(\mathrm{logit}\,\phi_t - \beta)\), where \(\phi_t\) is the proportion among verified subjects, so \(\beta\) links the two groups but the data say nothing about it: its posterior equals its prior (Gustafson, 2015). The prior on \(\beta\) is then an explicit assumption, and varying it, or fixing \(\beta\) at a range of values, shows how much the results depend on it (Buzoianu and Kadane, 2008; Kosinski and Barnhart, 2003b).

With the log-linear (Baker, 1995) and random-effects (Dendukuri and Joseph, 2001; Qu et al., 1996) disease models, \(\beta\) is identified through the restrictions that these models place on the disease distribution. This information comes from the assumed structure, not from the data alone, and it is fragile if the structure is wrong (Albert and Dodd, 2004).

References

Albert, P. S. and Dodd, L. E. (2004). A cautionary note on the robustness of latent class models for estimating diagnostic error without a gold standard. Biometrics, 60(2), 427–435. doi:10.1111/j.0006-341X.2004.00187.x

Baker, S. G. (1995). Evaluating multiple diagnostic tests with partial verification. Biometrics, 51(1), 330–337. doi:10.2307/2533339

Buzoianu, M. and Kadane, J. B. (2008). Adjusting for verification bias in diagnostic test evaluation: A Bayesian approach. Statistics in Medicine, 27(13), 2453–2473. doi:10.1002/sim.3099

Dendukuri, N. and Joseph, L. (2001). Bayesian approaches to modeling the conditional dependence between multiple diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 57(1), 158–167. doi:10.1111/j.0006-341X.2001.00158.x

Gustafson, P. (2015). Bayesian Inference for Partially Identified Models: Exploring the Limits of Limited Data. Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, FL.

Kosinski, A. S. and Barnhart, H. X. (2003a). Accounting for nonignorable verification bias in assessment of diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 59(1), 163–171. doi:10.1111/1541-0420.00019

Kosinski, A. S. and Barnhart, H. X. (2003b). A global sensitivity analysis of performance of a medical diagnostic test when verification bias is present. Statistics in Medicine, 22(17), 2711–2721. doi:10.1002/sim.1517

Qu, Y., Tan, M. and Kutner, M. H. (1996). Random effects models in latent class analysis for evaluating accuracy of diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 52(3), 797–810. doi:10.2307/2533043

See also

mar(), verification_mechanism, sensitivity_analysis()

Examples

mnar()
#> <mnar> verification depends on the test results and on the disease
#>   odds_ratio_prior: Normal(mean = 0, sd = 1)
#>   intercepts_prior: Normal(mean = 0, sd = 1.5)
mnar(odds_ratio_prior = prior_normal(mean = log(2), sd = 0.5))
#> <mnar> verification depends on the test results and on the disease
#>   odds_ratio_prior: Normal(mean = 0.6931, sd = 0.5)
#>   intercepts_prior: Normal(mean = 0, sd = 1.5)
